extracted.intended_audience: founders of early-stage startups and small startup PR/marketing teams
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, founder-centered guidance for planning and executing media relations and product launches at early-stage startups without an agency. Covers when to hire help, how to craft messaging, timing and launch runway, building reporter relationships, and founder media behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be able to clearly answer 'what do you actually do?' before doing PR
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can’t answer what you do in clear terms, don’t do anything else until you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hammerling: “If you can’t answer that question, don’t do anything else until you can. Nothing else matters.” Use basic questions (What are you? Why are you? Who are you? What problem are you solving and how?) to reach clarity. If stakeholders give different answers, reconcile them before outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to retain a PR firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Only three early-stage scenarios justify hiring a PR firm: entering a crowded market, being very disruptive, or involving a legacy CEO with press history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: “There are only three reasons an early-stage company should consider retaining the services of a firm: It’s entering a crowded market; It’s a very disruptive company; There’s a legacy CEO involved who has history with the press.” Otherwise spend on product and team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate stakeholders to discover your narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview founders, key team members and investors separately to hear different framings of the company and identify overlaps that form a narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for who phrases things succinctly vs. who grasps longer narrative; combine the best elements to form a coherent story and messaging hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a concise messaging document
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a top-line one-sentence message, then three key messages for reporters and more detailed layers beneath; distribute to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the most succinct resonant messaging at the top — “what you want to say at cocktail parties.” Under that place three key messages, then supporting detail. Make sure everyone has a copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR is about focusing your voice, not raw hits or placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure PR success by clarity and position in market, not simply media mentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: “PR isn’t about hits and it isn’t about placement. It’s about focusing your voice. It’s about finding your place in the market.” Avoid treating PR as one-off bump chasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify messaging; avoid jargon and long-winded explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Boil down complex or technical offerings into one main, relatable idea that mainstream press and users can understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example NetSuite: remove jargon and tell the one main thing. Don’t try to explain entire technical stacks in early press; help people imagine themselves using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid analogies as primary branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies like 'It’s like X only for Y' can be instructive but weaken brand distinctiveness if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boil your message to its core first, then layer in dimensions and functionality later rather than relying on comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t pack every feature into one announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight the single key thing your product does; layer additional features later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: “You may do 25 things and that’s amazing, but what’s that key thing you do?” Packing everything into one release will lose your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow a 3–6 month runway for a solid media plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective media planning typically requires three to six months; last-minute turnkey strategies rarely work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hammerling: “A solid media plan needs a runway of three to six months.” If you only have weeks, the launch will likely look fake and be ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure product readiness; don’t launch before it works
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid launching before the product is ready; premature launches cause bad press and setbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If product isn’t ready, pull the marketing plug. Example: many startups stick to timelines and release faulty products, setting them back months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify PR goals to guide targeting and messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about whether the goal is attention, users, recruiting, or raising capital; the goal shapes outlets and pitch style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Do you want attention early on? Attract users/customers? Recruit talent? Raise capital? Tailor outreach (e.g., Reddit/Hacker News for engineers; investor-targeted pubs for VCs). Be transparent about goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid timing your product launch with a funding announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate funding news from product messaging; leading with funding skews expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: “If you need to announce funding, try to separate it as much as you can from your product. Absolutely don’t lead with it.” A large round raises expectations that may hurt product reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read reporters’ work and craft personalized outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who covers your space, study their past writing (including older pieces), and personalize outreach to fit their interests and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow reporters on Twitter to learn passions and personality. Use that knowledge to craft tailored communications rather than mass pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate relationships with a meaningful handful of reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Forge and maintain relationships with several reporters in your area and complementary coverage areas, including younger reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hammerling began by knowing 15 influential reporters; getting to know younger, entrepreneurial reporters matters because they may be future influencers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t be afraid to reach out in person — but only when message is ready
rubrics_metrics.description: You can ask to meet or grab coffee with reporters, but do so after your message is clear and avoid tipping your hand too early to those you’ll pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop a note a few weeks before you’re in town. Don’t talk to reporters too far in advance of launch to avoid leaking the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exclusives sparingly; avoid for routine early-stage launches
rubrics_metrics.description: Early-stage companies should generally avoid offering exclusives because it hurts broader relationships; use exclusives primarily for damage control when a reporter uncovers a story early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive can be appropriate if a reporter uncovers a story and you need time: offer a short delay and gratitude. Routine exclusive use creates 'bad blood' with other journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in media training to learn interview skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Media trainers teach founders how to answer questions succinctly and perform on interviews; small, focused training can be effective without hiring an agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hammerling recommends hiring a trainer for even a half-day session. If unaffordable, study videos of strong presenters (e.g., Marc Benioff, Larry Ellison) to learn delivery, humor, and presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founders should be the primary media voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters want to connect to the founder’s story; founder involvement builds authenticity and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hammerling often refuses clients if founders won’t be actively involved. Founder blog posts are increasingly preferred over impersonal press releases because they feel authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be an area expert while remaining respectful about competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Know your competitive space deeply to be a useful resource, but avoid trash-talking competitors; position yourself via respected big companies instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asked about competitors, cite big, successful players to connect your startup to known success rather than naming and belittling small rivals. ‘Negativity never wins.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional: don’t pester reporters or respond personally to criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repeatedly asking if a story will run, attacking writers, or showing unprofessional behavior in public or social channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters remember founders who are difficult; writers take things personally. Never attack someone publicly for coverage mistakes — it creates long memories and harms future relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define relationship terms and understand 'off the record' vs 'on background'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about what is off the record, on background, or on the record; don’t give information and later retract the terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entrepreneurs must know and respect these terms to avoid burning relationships. Clarity prevents awkward situations where information is misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid becoming too chummy with journalists to the point of impaired judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendly relationships are fine, but being overly close can blind you and hurt the quality of stories you get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define boundaries so friendship doesn’t replace professional PR thinking. Close relationships sometimes fail to produce strong stories because of lack of critical focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor comments and social feedback; use them to refine messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader comments and social responses reveal what resonates or repels; use this data to hone product messaging or consider product changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If users praise an aspect, lean into it. If criticism surfaces consistently, consider clarifying messaging or altering the product. Don’t take comments personally; extract takeaways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project passion and personality in media appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders who are energetic, enjoy speaking, and show personality perform better in media than glum or robotic speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study exemplars (e.g., Aaron Levie) for fluidity, humor, and forward-looking statements. Being authentic and having fun helps enthrall media audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messaging and channels to specific audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweak your core message slightly to suit different audiences (engineers, investors, recruits) and choose corresponding channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use Reddit/Hacker News for hiring engineers; pitch investor-read publications to reach VCs. Stick with one overarching message but adapt phrasing per audience.
